query: Consider the following context: The combination of elevated temperature and tribo-corrosion leads to the accelerated degradation of structural components used in many extreme environments. Recently developed high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with multiple principal elements have the potential for superior degradation resistance compared with presently used structural alloys. In that context, which material can be used for superior tribo-corrosion degradation resistance, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Tuning the surface chemistry of an AlCoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloy by adjusting the concentrations of oxide-forming elements (e.g., Al, Ti, and Cr) will promote the in situ formation of a protective spinel-type oxide layer at elevated temperatures under friction, thereby significantly reducing tribo-corrosion degradation compared to conventional alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast or conventionally processed AlCoCrFeNi-based HEA without specifically engineered surface compositions.
generation.intervention: Surface/interface engineering via controlled adjustments of the oxide‐forming element ratios (particularly Al, Ti, and Cr) in the HEA composition to optimize the formation of a durable protective spinel oxide scale during operation.
generation.conditions: Exposure to extreme environments where elevated temperatures and mechanical friction act simultaneously in a corrosive environment (tribo-corrosion conditions).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and stability of a continuous, in situ spinel-type oxide layer on the alloy surface that acts as a barrier to both mechanical wear and corrosive attack.
generation.mechanism: The modified surface composition enhances the thermodynamic driving force for the formation of a stable and self-healing oxide layer during service. This layer effectively decouples the interface from aggressive environments, reducing both friction-induced material removal and corrosive dissolution.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable reduction in wear rate and corrosion loss under tribo-corrosion conditions, resulting in enhanced service life and performance compared to conventional structural alloys or HEAs without the tailored surface chemistry.
generation.baseline: Conventional structural alloys or HEAs that lack the specifically engineered surface chemistry typically exhibit accelerated degradation under combined elevated temperature and tribo-corrosion conditions.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected to be most pronounced in environments where temperatures are sufficiently high to activate the in situ oxidation process but below the threshold where phase instability or oxide spallation compromises the oxide layer integrity.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the long-term stability and adherence of the engineered oxide layer under cyclic or variable tribo-corrosive stresses, and the optimal compositional window (Al/Ti/Cr ratios) may require further refinement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of AlCoCrFeNi-based HEA samples: one with standard composition and one with the tailored oxide-forming element ratios (optimized Al/Ti/Cr) designed to promote spinel formation. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature tribo-corrosion testing using a controlled tribometer coupled with a corrosive atmosphere chamber. Monitor the evolution of surface oxide phases in situ and characterize the wear and corrosion rates over time.
measurements: Surface composition and phase analysis via XRD and electron microscopy to verify the formation and continuity of the spinel oxide layer.
Wear rate and corrosion loss measurements (e.g., mass loss, profilometry) under set tribo-corrosion conditions.
Adhesion and durability tests of the oxide scale (e.g., scratch testing or cyclic loading).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tailored HEA samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear and corrosion compared to the standard HEA samples, or if the spinel oxide layer is not observed or fails rapidly under test conditions, then the hypothesis that surface engineering in this manner improves tribo-corrosion resistance is falsified.

Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr 2 O 3 ), alumina (Al 2 O 3 ) or silica (SiO 2 ) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation [1] – [3] . However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components [1] , [2] . The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.

Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ]. decision.trend: Initial work on high-entropy alloys focused on bulk phase stability and mechanical performance under extreme conditions. For instance, studies on AlCoCrFeNi‐based systems (such as the AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 alloy) demonstrated that at elevated temperatures, the alloy’s multiphase microstructure can evolve to form oxide phases (like spinel) that improve wear resistance. While these works addressed high‐temperature wear (or corrosion) individually relative to conventional alloys, the combined degradation mechanism—tribo‐corrosion under extreme thermal and friction conditions—remains only partly mitigated.
decision.unsolved: The integrated challenge of tribo‐corrosion (where mechanical wear and corrosive degradation act synergistically) has not yet been fully resolved. In particular, controlling the surface reactivity and ensuring the formation of a durable, protective oxide layer during service remain open issues.
decision.lever: tailoring the surface chemistry to promote in situ formation of stable, protective oxide (spinel) layers via controlled adjustments in the oxide‐forming elements (e.g., optimized Al/Ti/Cr ratios) within the HEA.
decision.why: Because preceding studies indicate that HEAs like AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 can benefit from the development of a dual-phase microstructure that forms protective oxides at high temperatures, it is most plausible to next leverage surface/interface engineering. This focused approach aims to further stabilize and control the formation of beneficial oxide scales that directly counteract both wear and corrosion, precisely addressing the tribo‐corrosion degradation observed in extreme operating conditions.
